bp: A technology-assisted review system is built for a very practical kind of overload: a large collection contains a small set of documents that people truly need to find, and missing those documents is costly. In legal discovery, systematic literature review, and Web-scale information access, the goal is not merely to show a few pleasing results. The goal is high recall: bring as many relevant items as possible into view so experts can make defensible decisions. ALTARS 2026 treats this as a Web problem because the Web is no longer a neat pile of English pages. It contains changing documents, many languages, user-made material, and AI-produced text. The workshop asks how review systems can combine machine help with human judgment while remaining transparent, reliable, and fair. Its object is therefore not one ranking model, but the whole review workflow: retrieval, screening, explanation, governance, and adaptation as the collection changes.
wh: The hard part is that review work has two competing demands. The system must shrink a huge pile quickly, but it must not silently discard the rare items that matter. A normal search engine can tolerate some missed pages if the top results satisfy the user. A high-recall review system cannot rely on that bargain, because the missing item may be the legal document, medical study, policy record, or Web evidence that changes the conclusion. Web collections add more trouble. Documents arrive and disappear, languages mix, sources vary in reliability, and AI-produced content can make text look fluent without making it trustworthy. Human reviewers also have limited time, so the system must decide what to ask them to inspect. The abstract emphasizes transparency, fairness, and reliability because automated review can otherwise become a hidden gatekeeper: it decides what humans never see, while giving too little explanation for why those decisions were made.
naive: A smart beginner might first index every document, run a keyword search, sort by an automatic relevance score, and ask reviewers to inspect results from the top downward. That is attractive because it matches familiar Web search. It fails when the relevant documents use different words, appear in another language, come from unfamiliar formats, or are mixed with generated content that imitates the topic. It also fails because a high score is not the same as a complete review. If the system cannot explain why items were promoted or skipped, reviewers cannot tell whether the process is fair, whether a group of documents was missed, or whether the machine is repeating biased patterns from earlier review decisions.
ap: The central move in ALTARS 2026 is to treat technology-assisted review as augmented intelligence rather than as replacement judgment. The machine should not simply return a final answer; it should help people search, prioritize, explain, and revise the review process. In concrete terms, the workshop points to systems where retrieval models propose likely useful documents, humans provide feedback, explanations show why a document was selected, and governance rules check whether the process is reliable and fair. Large language models can help interpret varied text and generate review support, while knowledge graphs can organize entities and relations so evidence is not just a loose list of passages. The important design shift is workflow-level: the review system must support trustworthy iteration over a changing Web collection, not just produce a ranked page once. The paper is best read as a map of open research problems in that direction.
mech: The implied mechanism starts with a collection of Web documents or records that may differ by topic, source, language, format, and time. The review team has an information need, such as finding all legally responsive documents or all studies relevant to a systematic review. A retrieval component first turns that need into candidate documents to inspect. Instead of assuming the first ranking is final, the workflow brings human reviewers into the loop: reviewers judge selected documents, correct mistakes, and give the system evidence about what counts as relevant. The system then updates which documents should be brought forward next. If language models are used, they may help read, summarize, or compare difficult text, but their outputs need to be checked because fluent generated explanations can still be wrong. If knowledge graphs are used, entities, topics, sources, and relationships can be arranged as connected facts, letting the system follow related evidence instead of matching words alone. Explainable components expose the reasons behind selections, such as which text, relation, source cue, or prior reviewer signal mattered. Governance components ask whether the process is auditable, fair across languages or groups, and stable as the Web changes. The output is not only a ranked set of documents; it is a review trail showing what was found, what was judged, what remains uncertain, and why stopping or continuing would be defensible.
math: Several mathematical ideas sit underneath this agenda. Ranking is the first: each document is given a score so the system can decide which few deserve human attention first. The score is not truth; it is a sorting handle made from text match, source clues, language cues, prior judgments, or graph relations. The danger is that compressing many reasons into one order can hide why a document was buried. Probability is the second idea. In high-recall review, the team wants to know how much of the relevant material has probably been found, even though the unseen pile has not been fully judged. That requires measured uncertainty rather than a confident guess. Learning from human feedback is another idea: the system reuses patterns from reviewer decisions, but must avoid treating early or biased judgments as permanent truth. Graph reasoning adds structured evidence movement. Nodes might be documents, entities, topics, authors, claims, or sources; links say that two pieces of evidence are related. Following links can reveal useful documents that word matching misses, but bad or stale links can spread error. The core tradeoff across these ideas is speed versus completeness, with trust as a constraint: save review effort without hiding uncertainty, unfairness, or unsupported machine reasoning.
dots: This paper connects most directly to the conference's broader retrieval and ranking work, because TAR is a severe version of choosing a useful subset from a huge pile. It differs from ordinary search because the cost of a missed relevant item is central, not incidental. It also connects to the neighboring TAR stopping paper in the repo, which focuses on estimating recall early by combining a ranker with a probability sample; ALTARS describes the larger workshop agenda in which that kind of stopping decision belongs. The biomedical screening paper is another sibling: it also uses language models in a human-in-the-loop review setting, but for extracting patient, intervention, and outcome information from full-text studies. Knowledge graph papers are nearby because ALTARS names graph integration as a way to organize review evidence by entities and relations instead of loose text. Responsible AI and data governance are not side topics here; they are part of the retrieval task because transparency and fairness determine whether the review process can be trusted.
ww: The agenda works as a research direction because it matches the actual shape of review work. Reviewers do not need a machine that confidently replaces them; they need a machine that spends their attention well and leaves a record they can inspect. Ranking helps because relevant documents are usually not spread randomly. They share words, topics, citations, entities, sources, or relations that can be learned from examples. Human feedback helps because the meaning of relevance is often task-specific: what matters in one legal matter or literature review may not matter in another. Explanations help because they let reviewers catch the system when it is relying on the wrong signal, such as language, source popularity, or generated phrasing instead of substantive relevance. Language models can broaden the system's reading ability across messy Web text, while knowledge graphs can preserve relationships that simple keyword matching misses. The combination should beat the naive approach when each component is used with checks: machine triage for scale, human judgment for meaning, explanation for accountability, and governance for fairness.
po: The payoff is a clearer research path for trustworthy Web-scale review. ALTARS 2026 brings together information retrieval, Web science, artificial intelligence, and data governance around systems that can search large heterogeneous collections while keeping people in control. The capabilities it points toward are practical: finding more relevant material under limited review time, adapting to dynamic and multilingual Web content, using language models and knowledge graphs without giving up auditability, and making automated review decisions more transparent and fair. Because this is a workshop abstract, the concrete result is not a measured accuracy gain; it is a venue and agenda for shaping the next generation of TAR systems.
limits: The abstract does not prove that any specific TAR system is reliable, fair, multilingual, or Web-scale in deployment. It names important components, including human-in-the-loop learning, explainable AI, language models, knowledge graphs, and governance, but does not specify an implemented pipeline, dataset, evaluation protocol, or failure analysis. The agenda assumes reviewers can provide useful feedback, explanations can be made understandable, and graph or language-model support can be checked rather than blindly trusted. It also assumes fairness can be operationalized across sources, languages, and groups. Those are hard conditions. Without careful measurement, augmented review can still miss rare evidence, inherit biased judgments, overtrust generated text, or create transparency that looks persuasive without being truly diagnostic.
